lesson.title: A Quarter Million Voices: The March for Jobs and Freedom
lesson.summary: On August 28, 1963, roughly 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial to demand civil rights legislation and economic justice, and Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech.
lesson.body:
By the summer of 1963, the civil rights movement had gained enormous national attention thanks in large part to the Birmingham Campaign that spring. When Birmingham's police, under Commissioner Bull Connor, turned dogs and fire hoses on peaceful demonstrators, including children, the images shocked much of the country and pushed President John F. Kennedy to propose a sweeping civil rights bill in June 1963. Movement leaders decided that a mass demonstration in the nation's capital could keep pressure on Congress to pass it.

The event, officially called the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, was about more than pending legislation. Its name signaled two goals at once: an end to legal discrimination, and economic demands like fair wages and access to jobs. The idea drew on an older tradition. Back in 1941, labor leader A. Philip Randolph had threatened a march on Washington to protest discrimination in defense industries, a threat that persuaded President Franklin Roosevelt to issue an executive order banning it. In 1963, Randolph teamed with Bayard Rustin, a brilliant organizer and strategist of nonviolent protest, to build a coalition of six major civil rights organizations, often called the "Big Six": Randolph, Martin Luther King Jr. of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, Roy Wilkins of the NAACP, Whitney Young of the Urban League, James Farmer of the Congress of Racial Equality, and John Lewis of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee.

Rustin's role mattered in its own right. As an openly gay man and a former member of the Communist Party, he faced pressure from within the movement itself, with some leaders worried his background would be used to discredit the march. Randolph insisted on him anyway, and Rustin's meticulous planning, covering everything from transportation to first aid stations, helped make the march an orderly, peaceful model of mass demonstration.

On the day itself, an estimated 250,000 people, Black and white, gathered peacefully at the Lincoln Memorial, the largest demonstration Washington had seen up to that point. Several speakers addressed the crowd, including John Lewis, whose speech on the movement's unfinished business was toned down from his original draft after other leaders raised concerns about its sharper language. The day is remembered above all for King's closing address, in which he described his dream of a nation that would live out the true meaning of its founding creed, a nation where his children would one day be judged by the content of their character rather than the color of their skin, weaving together the language of the Declaration of Independence, the Bible, and American patriotic tradition.

The march did not by itself pass any law. But its disciplined, peaceful character undercut segregationist claims that civil rights activism led only to disorder, and it kept public and congressional attention focused on the civil rights bill Kennedy had proposed, a bill that would become law within the year.
